gap: No result ChatGPT got states that OtterBox's '7X military standard' counts drops, not height. OtterBox's VP of Engineering says it means the MIL-STD-810G 516.6 test run seven times, 'over 180 drops', and that test drops from 48 in (4 ft). UAG's '25 ft' is a drop height. The two numbers measure different things, so they can't be ranked against each other, and the Defender's '7X' never says it was dropped from higher than 4 ft.
standout_why: I compared against rottenwifi.com's '8 Best Protective Phone Cases of 2026' (cited in the second chat), which copies the Travel + Leisure picks, and against the d3j1zw3ygsdrnm.cloudfront.net 'Best Rugged Phone Cases' page. Rottenwifi says OtterBox offers 'up to seven-times military-grade drop protection' and gives 'no specific height'. It warns in general terms that ratings measure different things, but it never works out what 7X means. The cloudfront page says OtterBox claims 7X 'without naming the test', which is wrong: OtterBox names 810G-516.6. Neither page turns 7X into about 182 drops from 4 ft, and neither notes that UAG's own '5X MIL-SPEC' doesn't match its 25 ft as a height multiple (5 × 4 ft = 20 ft). I couldn't open the pages ChatGPT cited directly: Travel + Leisure and Good Housekeeping blocked the fetch tool. So whether they spell this out is judged only from rottenwifi's summary of T+L (four-foot and eight-foot editorial drops, no decoding of maker ratings).
decides: It confirms the Defender Series Pro as the pick for repeated everyday drops, since its claim is about surviving many drops from 4 ft. It takes away any claim that it beats the UAG Monarch Pro on drop height, because OtterBox publishes no height. A shopper worried about one long fall can only rely on UAG's stated 25 ft, which is UAG's own 'independently tested' claim with no lab or surface named. UAG's US store today lists the Monarch Pro for iPhone 17 at $42.95, compare-at $84.95, against the $79.95 ChatGPT showed. The SUPCASE UB Pro product page states no drop height at all, only a CNET drop-test win, and says it does NOT support MagSafe. That matters if the shopper uses MagSafe accessories.

findings.label: MIL-STD-810 Method 516.6 transit drop as described by a case maker
findings.value: 26 drops from 48 in (1.22 m) onto a Type III surface: 6 faces, 8 corners, 12 edges
findings.source_title: Understanding Military-Grade Standards in Phone Cases (SUPCASE)
findings.note: SUPCASE gives this for the 810H wording of Method 516.6 and says 810G and 810H are 'document revisions, not consumer protection tiers'. The page also mislabels the method once as 516.8. This is the baseline every 'NX military standard' multiplier refers to.

findings.label: Maker drop rating and what '7X' means
findings.value: '7X tested to military drop standard (810G-516.6)', which OtterBox's VP of Engineering says means the test survived seven times, 'over 180 drops'. No drop height stated.
findings.note: Quote attributed to Doug Kempel, VP of Engineering at Otter Products. 7 × 26 drops = 182, which matches 'over 180', so 7X multiplies the number of drops. At the standard's 48 in height, that means about 182 drops from 4 ft. OtterBox publishes no greater height.

findings.product: UAG Monarch Pro (iPhone 17 Pro Max; same text on the iPhone 17 Pro Kevlar and limited-edition pages)
findings.label: Maker drop rating
findings.value: '25 ft. Drop Protection: Independently tested to withstand drops up to 25 feet (7.6 meters)' plus 'Passes 5X MIL-SPEC 810G-516.6'
findings.source_title: Monarch Pro iPhone 17 Pro Max Case (UAG store)
findings.note: Read through storecheck.py; the text got cut off before the 5X phrase on this page, but the full phrase appears on the forged-carbon iPhone 17 Pro Max page. 25 ft is 6.25 × the standard's 4 ft, so '5X' can't be a height multiple. If it counts drops it would be 5 × 26 = 130, but UAG doesn't define it. No lab, surface or drop count is given for the 25 ft figure.
